ACAD.name: Acadia National Park
ACAD.summary: Acadia National Park was established in 1919 as Lafayette National Park — the first national park east of the Mississippi River — and renamed Acadia in 1929. Located on Mount Desert Island and surrounding areas along the Maine coast, the park protects roughly 49,000 acres of granite-peaked mountains, rocky shoreline, woodlands, and glacially carved lakes. George B. Dorr and Charles W. Eliot led the private land conservation effort that made the park possible, with John D. Rockefeller Jr. later financing the construction of 45 miles of carriage roads. The park's diverse ecosystems mark the overlap of northern boreal and eastern deciduous forests, supporting over 1,100 plant species and serving as a critical stopover for migratory birds along the Atlantic Flyway.

AMIS.name: Amistad National Recreation Area
AMIS.summary: Amistad National Recreation Area was authorized by Congress in 1965 and established in 1990 along the U.S.–Mexico border near Del Rio, Texas. The recreation area surrounds Amistad Reservoir, a 64,860-acre international lake formed by the Amistad Dam on the Rio Grande, built jointly by the United States and Mexico. The region contains some of the oldest and best-preserved rock art in North America, with over 200 known pictograph sites created by hunter-gatherer peoples over a span of roughly 4,000 years. The Fate Bell Shelter and Panther Cave are among the most significant archaeological sites in the Lower Pecos Canyonlands.

ANDE.name: Andersonville NHS
ANDE.summary: Andersonville National Historic Site in southwestern Georgia preserves the site of Camp Sumter, the largest Confederate military prison during the Civil War. Operational from February 1864 to April 1865, the stockade held up to 32,000 Union prisoners of war in a space originally designed for 10,000, and nearly 13,000 died from disease, malnutrition, and exposure. The site was designated a national historic site in 1970 and also serves as home to the National Prisoner of War Museum, which honors all American prisoners of war throughout the nation's history. The adjacent Andersonville National Cemetery, established in 1865, remains an active national cemetery.

ANTI.name: Antietam National Battlefield
ANTI.summary: Antietam National Battlefield in Sharpsburg, Maryland, preserves the site of the Battle of Antietam, fought on September 17, 1862 — the bloodiest single day in American military history, with an estimated 23,000 casualties. The Union's strategic victory gave President Abraham Lincoln the political leverage to issue the preliminary Emancipation Proclamation five days later, fundamentally shifting the war's purpose to include the abolition of slavery. Established as a national battlefield site in 1890, the park encompasses approximately 3,230 acres of rolling farmland and includes landmarks such as Burnside Bridge, the Dunker Church, and Bloody Lane.

ARCH.name: Arches National Park
ARCH.summary: Arches National Park in eastern Utah protects over 2,000 natural stone arches — the densest concentration of such formations in the world — along with pinnacles, balanced rocks, and eroded sandstone fins. The landscape was shaped over 300 million years as salt deposits, sandstone layers, and erosion created the park's distinctive red-rock formations. Originally proclaimed a national monument by President Herbert Hoover in 1929, it was redesignated as a national park in 1971. Delicate Arch, the park's most iconic feature, has become a widely recognized symbol of Utah and appears on the state's license plates.

ARHO.name: Arlington House, The Robert E. Lee Memorial
ARHO.summary: Arlington House was built between 1803 and 1818 by George Washington Parke Custis, the grandson of Martha Washington, as a memorial to George Washington. His daughter, Mary Anna Custis, married Robert E. Lee there in 1831, and the couple lived at the estate for 30 years before Lee resigned his U.S. Army commission to join the Confederacy in 1861. Union forces occupied the property early in the Civil War, and in 1864 the grounds were designated as a military cemetery — the origin of Arlington National Cemetery. The mansion was designated a national memorial in 1955 and is managed by the National Park Service in partnership with Arlington National Cemetery.

BISC.name: Biscayne National Park
BISC.summary: Biscayne National Park in southeastern Florida protects 172,971 acres of marine and coastal environments, making it one of the largest marine parks in the National Park System. Ninety-five percent of the park is water, encompassing Biscayne Bay, the northernmost Florida Keys, and a portion of the third-largest barrier reef in the world. Originally established as Biscayne National Monument in 1968 after a citizen-led campaign blocked a proposed industrial seaport, it was redesignated as a national park in 1980. The park preserves mangrove shorelines, the shallow waters of Biscayne Bay, the undeveloped upper Florida Keys, and living coral reefs supporting over 600 species of fish.

BLRI.name: Blue Ridge Parkway
BLRI.summary: The Blue Ridge Parkway stretches 469 miles along the crest of the Blue Ridge Mountains, connecting Shenandoah National Park in Virginia to Great Smoky Mountains National Park in North Carolina. Construction began in 1935 as a New Deal public works project and was not completed until 1987 with the opening of the Linn Cove Viaduct. Designed as a recreational motor road with no commercial vehicles allowed, the parkway passes through some of the oldest mountains in the world — the southern Appalachians — and features over 200 overlooks with sweeping views of the Blue Ridge. It is consistently the most-visited unit of the National Park System, drawing over 15 million recreational visitors annually.

BLSC.name: Blackwell School National Historic Site
BLSC.summary: Blackwell School National Historic Site in Marfa, Texas, was established on November 11, 2022, as the 423rd unit of the National Park System. The school operated from the 1880s through 1965 as the segregated school for Mexican American children in the Marfa Independent School District during the era of "Juan Crow" discrimination in Texas. Students were punished for speaking Spanish and faced systematic educational inequality. The site was championed by former students and their descendants — known as the Blackwell School Alliance — who preserved the remaining adobe classroom building and shared their oral histories to ensure this chapter of civil rights history would not be forgotten.

BRCA.name: Bryce Canyon National Park
BRCA.summary: Bryce Canyon National Park in southwestern Utah is renowned for its extraordinary collection of hoodoos — tall, thin spires of rock formed by frost weathering and stream erosion of the Claron Formation limestone. Despite its name, Bryce Canyon is not a true canyon but rather a series of natural amphitheaters carved into the eastern edge of the Paunsaugunt Plateau. The area was designated a national monument in 1923 and became a national park in 1928. The Paiute people, who inhabited the region for centuries before European contact, called the hoodoos "red rocks standing like men in a bowl-shaped canyon" in their oral tradition.

BUIS.name: Buck Island Reef National Monument
BUIS.summary: Buck Island Reef National Monument protects a small uninhabited island and its surrounding coral reef ecosystem located 1.5 miles off the northeast coast of St. Croix in the U.S. Virgin Islands. President John F. Kennedy established the monument in 1961, and it was expanded by President Bill Clinton in 2001 to encompass 19,015 acres of submerged lands. The monument's barrier reef — one of the finest in the Caribbean — includes an underwater snorkeling trail established by the National Park Service. The island itself supports dry tropical forest and serves as nesting habitat for endangered hawksbill and green sea turtles.

CACR.name: Cane River Creole National Historical Park
CACR.summary: Cane River Creole National Historical Park in Natchitoches Parish, Louisiana, preserves two 18th- and 19th-century Creole cotton plantations — Oakland and Magnolia — that document the complex history of French Creole culture, plantation agriculture, and enslaved labor along the Cane River. Established by Congress in 1994, the park protects plantation structures, slave quarters, agricultural landscapes, and the stories of the enslaved people who built and maintained these operations. The Cane River region is one of the oldest permanent European settlements in the Louisiana Purchase territory, and the park's cultural landscape reflects centuries of French, Spanish, African, and Native American influence.

CAHA.name: Cape Hatteras National Seashore
CAHA.summary: Cape Hatteras National Seashore, established in 1953, was the first national seashore in the United States. Stretching across portions of North Carolina's Outer Banks barrier islands — Bodie Island, Hatteras Island, and Ocracoke Island — the seashore protects over 30,000 acres of dynamic coastline shaped by wind, waves, and storms. The waters off Cape Hatteras, where the cold Labrador Current meets the warm Gulf Stream, have been known as the "Graveyard of the Atlantic" for the more than 1,000 shipwrecks documented in the area. The Cape Hatteras Lighthouse, at 198.5 feet the tallest brick lighthouse in the United States, was famously relocated 2,900 feet inland in 1999 to save it from shoreline erosion.

CANY.name: Canyonlands National Park
CANY.summary: Canyonlands National Park in southeastern Utah preserves 337,598 acres of dramatic desert landscape carved by the Colorado and Green Rivers into countless canyons, mesas, and buttes. Established as a national park in 1964 through the efforts of Secretary of the Interior Stewart Udall, Canyonlands is divided into four distinct districts: Island in the Sky, The Needles, The Maze, and the rivers themselves. The region's geological record spans over 300 million years, and archaeological evidence shows human presence dating back at least 10,000 years, including ancestral Puebloan granaries and Fremont rock art.

CARI.name: Cane River Creole National Historical Park
CARI.summary: Cane River Creole National Historical Park in Natchitoches Parish, Louisiana, preserves two 18th- and 19th-century Creole cotton plantations — Oakland and Magnolia — that document the complex history of French Creole culture, plantation agriculture, and enslaved labor along the Cane River. Established by Congress in 1994, the park protects plantation structures, slave quarters, agricultural landscapes, and the stories of the enslaved people who built and maintained these operations. The Cane River region is one of the oldest permanent European settlements in the Louisiana Purchase territory, and the park's cultural landscape reflects centuries of French, Spanish, African, and Native American influence.

CASA.name: Castillo de San Marcos National Monument
CASA.summary: Castillo de San Marcos National Monument in St. Augustine, Florida, preserves the oldest masonry fortification in the continental United States. Built by the Spanish between 1672 and 1695 using coquina — a local limestone formed from compressed shells — the fort was designed to protect Spain's claim to La Florida and the sea route of treasure ships returning to Europe. The fortress withstood multiple sieges, including British attacks in 1702 and 1740, and changed hands between Spain, Great Britain, the Confederate States, and the United States over its 300-year history. It was also used to imprison Native Americans, including members of the Seminole, Apache, Cheyenne, and other nations during the 19th century.

CAWO.name: Carter G. Woodson Home National Historic Site
CAWO.summary: The Carter G. Woodson Home National Historic Site in Washington, D.C., preserves the residence and workplace of Dr. Carter G. Woodson (1875–1950), the scholar known as the "Father of Black History." Woodson, the second African American to earn a Ph.D. from Harvard University (after W.E.B. Du Bois), founded the Association for the Study of Negro Life and History in 1915, established the Journal of Negro History in 1916, and created Negro History Week in 1926 — which later became Black History Month. He lived and worked in the Shaw neighborhood rowhouse from 1922 until his death in 1950. The site was designated a national historic site in 2006.

CHOH.name: C&O Canal NHP
CHOH.summary: The Chesapeake and Ohio Canal National Historical Park preserves the 184.5-mile towpath and canal route that runs from Georgetown in Washington, D.C. to Cumberland, Maryland, paralleling the Potomac River. Constructed between 1828 and 1850, the C&O Canal was conceived as a transportation route to connect the eastern seaboard with the Ohio River valley, but competition from the Baltimore and Ohio Railroad ultimately limited the canal's commercial success. The canal ceased operations in 1924 after a devastating flood, and a campaign led by Supreme Court Justice William O. Douglas in 1954 helped save the corridor from being converted into a highway. It was designated a national historical park in 1971.

CHPI.name: Charles Pinckney NHS
CHPI.summary: Charles Pinckney National Historic Site in Mount Pleasant, South Carolina, preserves the last known property associated with Charles Pinckney (1757–1824), a principal author and signer of the United States Constitution. Pinckney served as a delegate to the Constitutional Convention in 1787, where he submitted a comprehensive draft plan that influenced the final document, and later served as governor of South Carolina four times and as a U.S. senator and ambassador to Spain. The 28-acre site contains Snee Farm, a working plantation where enslaved African Americans labored for generations. The site was established in 1988 to tell the intertwined stories of Constitutional democracy and the enslaved people whose labor sustained the property.

CHRI.name: Christiansted National Historic Site
CHRI.summary: Christiansted National Historic Site on the island of St. Croix in the U.S. Virgin Islands preserves several colonial-era structures in the historic waterfront town of Christiansted, the former capital of the Danish West Indies. The site includes Fort Christiansvaern (built 1738–1749), the Danish West India and Guinea Company Warehouse, the Steeple Building, and the Scale House — all built during Denmark's colonial rule of the island from 1733 to 1917. The economy of Danish St. Croix was driven by sugar plantation agriculture dependent on the labor of enslaved Africans, who constituted the vast majority of the island's population. The site was designated in 1952 to preserve this colonial history and was one of the first NPS units in the Virgin Islands.

CUGA.name: Cumberland Gap NHP
CUGA.summary: Cumberland Gap National Historical Park straddles the border of Kentucky, Virginia, and Tennessee at a natural pass through the Appalachian Mountains that has served as a major migration corridor for thousands of years. Herds of bison and Native American peoples — including Cherokee and Shawnee — used the gap long before European settlement. In 1775, Daniel Boone led a party to widen the trail through the gap into what became the Wilderness Road, and by 1810 an estimated 200,000 to 300,000 settlers had passed through Cumberland Gap heading west. The park was authorized by Congress in 1940 and encompasses over 24,000 acres of forested mountain terrain.

CUIS.name: Cumberland Island National Seashore
CUIS.summary: Cumberland Island National Seashore protects Georgia's largest and southernmost barrier island — an 18-mile-long island encompassing over 36,000 acres of maritime forest, salt marshes, tidal creeks, and undeveloped beaches. The island has a layered human history stretching from the Timucuan people through Spanish missions, British colonial settlement, and the plantation era. After the Civil War, formerly enslaved people established the First African Baptist Church on the island, which still stands today. In the late 19th century, industrialist Thomas Carnegie and his wife Lucy built several grand estates on the island. The national seashore was established in 1972 to protect the island's natural and cultural resources from development.

EVER.name: Everglades NP
EVER.summary: Everglades National Park, established in 1947, protects 1.5 million acres of tropical and subtropical wetlands at the southern tip of Florida — the largest subtropical wilderness in the United States. It was the first national park created to protect a biological ecosystem rather than scenic grandeur. The park's "River of Grass," as described by Marjory Stoneman Douglas in her influential 1947 book, is a slow-moving sheet of water that flows southward from Lake Okeechobee to Florida Bay. The Everglades provides habitat for 36 federally listed threatened or endangered species, including the Florida panther, American crocodile, and West Indian manatee. It is designated as a UNESCO World Heritage Site, an International Biosphere Reserve, and a Wetland of International Importance.

FIIS.name: Fire Island National Seashore
FIIS.summary: Fire Island National Seashore, established in 1964, protects a 26-mile stretch of barrier island off the southern shore of Long Island, New York — one of the last remaining undeveloped barrier beaches on the Atlantic Coast. The national seashore was created after a fierce conservation battle to prevent large-scale resort development on the island. The park includes the Sunken Forest, a rare 300-year-old maritime holly forest growing behind the dunes, and the Fire Island Lighthouse, first constructed in 1826 and rebuilt in 1858. The William Floyd Estate, the ancestral home of a signer of the Declaration of Independence, is also part of the seashore. Fire Island has historically served as a significant cultural refuge for LGBTQ communities, particularly the communities of Cherry Grove and Fire Island Pines.

FODA.name: Fort Davis National Historic Site
FODA.summary: Fort Davis National Historic Site in the Davis Mountains of West Texas preserves one of the best surviving examples of a frontier military post in the American Southwest. Established in 1854, the fort guarded emigrants, mail coaches, and freight wagons on the San Antonio–El Paso road through Limpia Canyon. After the Civil War, the post was garrisoned by troops of the 9th and 10th U.S. Cavalry and the 24th and 25th U.S. Infantry — the famed Buffalo Soldiers, African American troops who played a vital role in the frontier Army during the Indian Wars period. The fort was active until 1891 and was designated a national historic site in 1963. Over two dozen original and restored buildings remain, making it one of the most intact frontier forts in the West.

FODO.name: Fort Donelson National Battlefield
FODO.summary: Fort Donelson National Battlefield in Dover, Tennessee, preserves the site of the first major Union victory in the Civil War. In February 1862, forces under Brigadier General Ulysses S. Grant captured the Confederate river fortification on the Cumberland River after a combined land and naval assault. The surrender of roughly 12,000 Confederate troops — the largest surrender of American forces up to that point — opened the door for Union control of middle and western Tennessee and earned Grant the nickname "Unconditional Surrender" Grant. The battlefield was established as a national military park in 1928 and redesignated a national battlefield in 1985.

FOFR.name: Fort Frederica National Monument
FOFR.summary: Fort Frederica National Monument on St. Simons Island, Georgia, preserves the archaeological remains of a fortified town founded in 1736 by James Edward Oglethorpe as the southern outpost of the British colony of Georgia. The settlement served as a military buffer between British Georgia and Spanish Florida during a period of intense colonial rivalry. In 1742, British troops from Frederica defeated a larger Spanish invasion force at the nearby Battle of Bloody Marsh — a decisive engagement that effectively ended Spain's attempts to reclaim Georgia. At its peak, Frederica was home to about 500 soldiers and civilians. The monument was established in 1936 to preserve the town's ruins and earthwork fortifications.

FOMC.name: Fort McHenry National Monument and Historic Shrine
FOMC.summary: Fort McHenry National Monument and Historic Shrine in Baltimore, Maryland, is the birthplace of the American national anthem. During the Battle of Baltimore on September 13–14, 1814, British naval forces bombarded the star-shaped fort for 25 hours during the War of 1812. The fort's successful defense inspired Francis Scott Key, who watched the bombardment from a truce ship in the harbor, to write the poem "Defence of Fort M'Henry," which was later set to music and became "The Star-Spangled Banner," officially adopted as the national anthem in 1931. Designated as a national park in 1925 and redesignated in 1939, Fort McHenry is the only unit in the National Park System designated both a national monument and a historic shrine.

FORA.name: Fort Raleigh NHS
FORA.summary: Fort Raleigh National Historic Site on Roanoke Island, North Carolina, preserves the site of England's first attempts to establish a permanent settlement in North America. Sir Walter Raleigh sponsored expeditions in 1585 and 1587 to colonize the area; the second expedition, led by John White, included 117 men, women, and children who established the famous "Lost Colony." When White returned from a supply trip to England in 1590, the colonists had vanished, leaving only the word "CROATOAN" carved into a post. The fate of the colonists remains one of American history's most enduring mysteries. The site was designated in 1941 and also commemorates the Freedmen's Colony established on Roanoke Island during the Civil War, where formerly enslaved people built a self-governing community.

FOSU.name: Fort Sumter and Fort Moultrie NHP
FOSU.summary: Fort Sumter and Fort Moultrie National Historical Park in Charleston Harbor, South Carolina, preserves the sites of the opening and closing engagements of the Civil War. On April 12, 1861, Confederate forces fired on the Union-held Fort Sumter, beginning the four-year conflict that would cost over 600,000 American lives. Fort Moultrie, on nearby Sullivan's Island, has an even longer military history — Patriot forces there repelled a British naval attack in 1776 during the Revolutionary War in one of the first decisive American victories. The park also interprets the role of Charleston Harbor as the main port of entry for enslaved Africans brought to North America, with an estimated 40 percent of all enslaved people entering the country passing through these waters.

FRRI.name: Freedom Riders National Monument
FRRI.summary: Freedom Riders National Monument in Anniston, Alabama, was designated by President Barack Obama in 2017 to preserve two sites associated with the 1961 Freedom Rides — the former Greyhound Bus Station in Anniston and the site outside the city where a mob firebombed a Greyhound bus carrying Freedom Riders on May 14, 1961. The Freedom Riders were interracial groups of civil rights activists who rode interstate buses into the segregated South to challenge the non-enforcement of Supreme Court rulings that declared segregated public buses unconstitutional. The brutal attacks in Anniston and Birmingham generated national and international outrage and ultimately led the Interstate Commerce Commission to enforce desegregation of interstate travel facilities.

GLAC.name: Glacier National Park
GLAC.summary: Glacier National Park in northwestern Montana protects over one million acres of pristine mountain landscape in the northern Rocky Mountains, including portions of two mountain ranges, over 130 named lakes, more than 1,000 species of plants, and hundreds of species of animals. Established as a national park in 1910 following advocacy by naturalist George Bird Grinnell, the park is known as the "Crown of the Continent" for its dramatic glacially carved terrain. Together with Waterton Lakes National Park in Alberta, Canada, it forms the Waterton-Glacier International Peace Park, the world's first international peace park, designated in 1932. The park's namesake glaciers have been shrinking due to climate change; of the approximately 150 glaciers present in 1850, only 25 named glaciers remained active as of recent scientific surveys. The Blackfeet Nation has deep ancestral ties to the eastern slopes of the park, which they know as the "Backbone of the World."

GLCA.name: Glen Canyon National Recreation Area
GLCA.summary: Glen Canyon National Recreation Area in southern Utah and northern Arizona encompasses over 1.25 million acres of desert canyon country surrounding Lake Powell, the reservoir created by Glen Canyon Dam on the Colorado River. The dam, completed in 1966, was one of the most controversial reclamation projects in American history — its construction flooded hundreds of miles of canyon and thousands of archaeological sites, galvanizing the modern environmental movement. Author and conservationist Edward Abbey's writings about the area, particularly "Desert Solitaire" (1968), helped bring national attention to the ecological costs of damming western rivers. The recreation area also protects Rainbow Bridge National Monument, one of the world's largest natural bridges, sacred to the Navajo, Paiute, and other Indigenous nations.

GRCA.name: Grand Canyon National Park
GRCA.summary: Grand Canyon National Park in northern Arizona protects 1,218,375 acres encompassing the most spectacular portion of the Grand Canyon — a 277-mile gorge carved by the Colorado River that exposes nearly two billion years of Earth's geological history. The canyon reaches depths of over a mile, with layered bands of colorful rock revealing the geological story of the North American continent. President Theodore Roosevelt, who first visited in 1903, declared it a national monument in 1908; it became a national park in 1919. Eleven Native American tribes, including the Havasupai, Hualapai, Navajo, and Hopi, have ancestral connections to the canyon. The Grand Canyon was designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1979 and receives over six million visitors annually.

GRSM.name: Great Smoky Mountains National Park
GRSM.summary: Great Smoky Mountains National Park, straddling the border of Tennessee and North Carolina, is the most visited national park in the United States, drawing over 12 million recreational visits annually. Established in 1934, the park protects 522,427 acres of old-growth temperate forest — one of the largest blocks of hardwood forest remaining in North America. The park's biodiversity is extraordinary: it is home to over 19,000 documented species and is often called the "Salamander Capital of the World" for its 30-plus salamander species. The Cherokee people inhabited the region for thousands of years before forced removal along the Trail of Tears in 1838; members of the Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians still reside on the adjacent Qualla Boundary. The park was designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1983 and an International Biosphere Reserve in 1976.

GRTE.name: Grand Teton National Park
GRTE.summary: Grand Teton National Park in northwestern Wyoming protects the Teton Range — one of the youngest mountain ranges in the Rocky Mountains, rising abruptly over 7,000 feet above the valley floor of Jackson Hole without foothills. The park was established in 1929, originally protecting only the mountains themselves, and was expanded in 1950 to include much of Jackson Hole valley after John D. Rockefeller Jr. quietly purchased and donated 35,000 acres of ranchland. The park encompasses glacial lakes, alpine meadows, and the headwaters of the Snake River, and supports wildlife populations including grizzly bears, wolves, bison, and one of the largest elk herds in North America. Together with adjacent Yellowstone National Park and surrounding national forests, Grand Teton is part of the Greater Yellowstone Ecosystem, one of the last remaining large, intact temperate ecosystems on Earth.

GWMP.name: George Washington Memorial Parkway
GWMP.summary: George Washington Memorial Parkway preserves the natural scenery along the Potomac River and connects significant historic sites from Mount Vernon, George Washington's estate in Virginia, through the nation's capital. The parkway was authorized by Congress in 1930 as a memorial to the first president and was designed as a scenic and recreational corridor. The park system encompasses over 7,000 acres across multiple sites in Virginia, Maryland, and the District of Columbia, including Great Falls Park, Theodore Roosevelt Island, the Claude Moore Colonial Farm site, and the historic town of Glen Echo. The parkway itself follows part of the route Washington traveled between his Mount Vernon plantation and what would become the federal city.

HAFE.name: Harpers Ferry National Historical Park
HAFE.summary: Harpers Ferry National Historical Park in West Virginia, Maryland, and Virginia preserves the town at the confluence of the Potomac and Shenandoah Rivers where abolitionist John Brown led his famous 1859 raid on the federal armory — a pivotal event that accelerated the nation's march toward civil war. Harpers Ferry changed hands eight times between Union and Confederate forces during the Civil War and witnessed the largest surrender of Union troops during the war in September 1862. After the war, Storer College — one of the first integrated schools in the United States — was established in the town to educate formerly enslaved people. The Niagara Movement, the precursor to the NAACP, held its second meeting at Storer College in 1906. The park was established in 1944.

HOBE.name: Horseshoe Bend National Military Park
HOBE.summary: Horseshoe Bend National Military Park in east-central Alabama preserves the site of the decisive battle of the Creek War. On March 27, 1814, forces led by General Andrew Jackson, including U.S. Army regulars, Tennessee militia, Cherokee allies, and Lower Creek warriors, attacked the fortified camp of the Red Stick Creek faction at a horseshoe-shaped bend on the Tallapoosa River. Approximately 800 of the 1,000 Red Stick warriors were killed in the battle — one of the deadliest defeats suffered by Native Americans in U.S. history. The resulting Treaty of Fort Jackson forced the Creek Nation to cede roughly 23 million acres — half of present-day Alabama and part of southern Georgia — to the United States. The park was established in 1956.

HUTR.name: Hubbell Trading Post National Historic Site
HUTR.summary: Hubbell Trading Post National Historic Site near Ganado, Arizona, preserves the oldest continuously operating trading post on the Navajo Nation. Established by John Lorenzo Hubbell in 1878, the post served as a vital center of commerce and cultural exchange between the Navajo people and the wider American economy. Hubbell became a trusted figure in the community, acting as interpreter, mediator, and advisor while building a business around Navajo weavings, silverwork, and other crafts. The trading post was designated a national historic site in 1965 and still functions as a working trading post today, selling Navajo rugs, jewelry, and pottery. The site preserves the Hubbell family home, a visitor center with historic rug collections, and the surrounding cultural landscape.

INDE.name: Independence National Historical Park
INDE.summary: Independence National Historical Park in Philadelphia, Pennsylvania, preserves several of the most historically significant buildings in the United States, including Independence Hall — where both the Declaration of Independence and the United States Constitution were debated and adopted — and the Liberty Bell. Independence Hall, a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1979, hosted the Second Continental Congress (1775–1783) and the Constitutional Convention of 1787. The park also includes Congress Hall, where the U.S. Congress met from 1790 to 1800 when Philadelphia served as the nation's capital, and the President's House site, which interprets the stories of the nine enslaved Africans George Washington brought to the executive mansion during his presidency.

INDU.name: Indiana Dunes National Park (National Lakeshore)
INDU.summary: Indiana Dunes National Park on the southern shore of Lake Michigan in northwestern Indiana protects 15,349 acres of dunes, wetlands, prairies, rivers, and forests. The park's origins trace to the early 20th-century conservation campaign led by botanist Henry Cowles, whose groundbreaking studies of plant succession on the Indiana dunes helped establish the modern science of ecology. Despite being surrounded by one of the most heavily industrialized regions in North America, the park supports remarkable biodiversity — over 1,100 native plant species, the fourth-highest count of any national park unit. Originally designated as Indiana Dunes National Lakeshore in 1966, it was redesignated as a national park in 2019.

JELA.name: Jean Lafitte National Historical Park and Preserve

LOWE.name: Lowell National Historical Park
LOWE.summary: Lowell National Historical Park in Lowell, Massachusetts, preserves and interprets the history of America's Industrial Revolution in the nation's first large-scale planned industrial city. In the 1820s, a group of Boston investors known as the Boston Manufacturing Company built a network of power canals and textile mills along the Merrimack River, creating a factory system that transformed American manufacturing. The mills employed thousands of young women — known as the "mill girls" — who left New England farms to work in the factories, representing one of the first large-scale entries of American women into the industrial workforce. The park was established in 1978 and preserves 5.6 miles of canals, operating gatehouses, and mill buildings in a model of urban industrial heritage preservation.

MACA.name: Mammoth Cave National Park
MACA.summary: Mammoth Cave National Park in central Kentucky protects the world's longest known cave system, with over 420 miles of surveyed passageways — more than twice the length of any other known cave. The cave was formed over millions of years as mildly acidic water dissolved the park's thick limestone bedrock. Native Americans explored and mined minerals in the cave at least 4,000 years ago, and during the War of 1812, enslaved laborers were forced to mine calcium nitrate (saltpeter) from the cave for use in gunpowder. Enslaved men, most notably Stephen Bishop, served as the cave's first guides in the 1830s and 1840s, making major explorations and mapping discoveries. The park was established in 1941 and was designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1981 and an International Biosphere Reserve in 1990.

MANA.name: Manassas National Battlefield Park
MANA.summary: Manassas National Battlefield Park in Prince William County, Virginia, preserves the site of two major Civil War battles. The First Battle of Bull Run (Manassas) on July 21, 1861, was the war's first major land engagement, shattering both sides' expectations of a quick conflict and earning Confederate General Thomas J. Jackson his famous nickname "Stonewall." The Second Battle of Manassas, fought August 28–30, 1862, was a decisive Confederate victory that brought Robert E. Lee's Army of Northern Virginia to the doorstep of Washington, D.C. and set the stage for Lee's first invasion of the North. The battlefield was designated a national battlefield park in 1940 and preserves approximately 5,000 acres of the historic landscape.

MEMY.name: Medgar and Myrlie Evers Home National Monument
MEMY.summary: Medgar and Myrlie Evers Home National Monument in Jackson, Mississippi, preserves the modest ranch-style house where civil rights leader Medgar Evers lived with his wife Myrlie and their three children. Evers served as the NAACP's first field secretary in Mississippi, organizing voter registration drives, economic boycotts, and investigations into racial violence during the height of the civil rights movement. On June 12, 1963, Evers was assassinated in his driveway by white supremacist Byron De La Beckwith — a murder that galvanized the civil rights movement and contributed to the passage of the Civil Rights Act of 1964. The site was designated a national monument by President Barack Obama in 2020. Myrlie Evers-Williams went on to become a prominent civil rights leader in her own right, serving as chair of the NAACP.

MONO.name: Monocacy National Battlefield
MONO.summary: Monocacy National Battlefield near Frederick, Maryland, preserves the site of the Battle of Monocacy, fought on July 9, 1864 — often called "The Battle That Saved Washington." When Confederate General Jubal Early led an army toward the Union capital, a hastily assembled force of Union soldiers under General Lew Wallace (later the author of "Ben-Hur") delayed Early's advance for an entire day at the Monocacy River crossing. Although the Union forces were defeated, the delay allowed reinforcements to reach Washington's defenses in time to prevent the capital's capture. The battlefield was established as a national battlefield in 1934 and preserves 1,647 acres of agricultural landscape and historic structures.

MORA.summary:
Mount Rainier is the tallest volcano in the Cascade Range and the most heavily glaciated peak in the continental United States, a 14,410-foot mountain whose rivers of ice run up to 750 feet deep while steam still escapes from vents at its summit. Below the ice the seasons are compressed: in the subalpine meadows summer may last only two months, and the wildflowers, insects, birds and mammals race through it before the snow returns. [1]

Archaeological findings suggest people have been coming to the mountain for more than 9,000 years. Congress made it the nation’s fifth national park on March 2, 1899, and in 1988 designated more than 97 percent of it as wilderness. Nearly two million people a year now walk its meadows and old-growth forest and sleep in rustic log-and-boulder lodges built a century ago, in a landscape the Park Service itself calls anything but permanent: ice and rock break away from the peak, rivers of meltwater and debris wreak havoc with roads and buildings, and the brochure handed to visitors concedes that as the planet warms, no one knows how the mountain’s plants, animals or visitors will fare. [1]

climate.html: The Nisqually Glacier, visible from the road to Paradise, has been watched longer than almost any glacier in America: its terminus was first recorded in 1857, and it has since retreated more than two and a quarter kilometres up the mountain. Weather stations at Longmire and Paradise show the forty-five years from 1970 to 2015 growing 1.5 °C warmer and 0.77 metres drier, and the glacier losing another 280 metres of length in that span; researchers expect it to keep shrinking unless the climate changes. The ice does not go quietly. Ten outburst floods have surged from the glacier in the period of record, nine of them during retreat, sending water and rock down the Nisqually toward the park’s roads and buildings. [4] [5]

indigenous.html:
Long before it was a park, the mountain was a late-summer destination. The ethnographer Allan H. Smith, whose 1960s fieldwork Catton reports (and partly questions), identified five peoples who used it — the Nisqually, Puyallup, Muckleshoot, Yakima (today’s Yakama Nation) and Taidnapam: families climbed from the lowland valleys and over the passes to camp in the high meadows when the huckleberries ripened, to hunt deer, elk and mountain goat, and occasionally to seek spirit power. Each fall they set fire to the meadows so the berry patches would spread — a practice park officials never understood and never continued. Early accounts rendered the mountain’s name as “Takhoma,” though Catton cautions that much of what settlers wrote about Indian belief was shaped to suit their own purposes. [2] [3]

The treaties of 1854 and 1855 that ceded this country reserved the privilege of hunting and gathering roots and berries on “open and unclaimed land,” but after 1899 park officials treated the mountain as closed. In 1915 the Interior Department’s solicitor concluded that the treaty right had survived the park’s creation; a year later the Park Service’s chief clerk advised that state law and two court decisions had superseded that opinion, and rangers kept enforcing the ban. In October 1917 six Yakima people — four men and two women, by the newspaper account Catton quotes — were arrested at Yakima Park with freshly skinned deer hides and fined. Catton’s conclusion is that the park amplified and distorted Indian legends at the same time as it altered Indian use of the mountain. Descendants of those nations still hold the mountain as a place of special connection today. [2] [1]

sources.title: Catton, Wonderland: An Administrative History of Mount Rainier National Park (1996), ch. 1, Historical Overview of Indians and Mount Rainier

labor_ccc.html: Much of what visitors still touch at Rainier — the stone guardrails, log cabins and campgrounds — was built by young men of the Depression. By mid-July 1933 more than a thousand Civilian Conservation Corps enrollees, single men aged 18 to 25 from families on relief, were at work in five park camps; many companies were shipped west by train, including three from New York and one from Illinois in the first season and, in 1937, a company of 140 from Arkansas. One crew spent 703 man-days on a single mile of trail past Narada Falls. The Corps was segregated nationally: Black enrollees were underrepresented and mostly formed into separate companies, and Native Americans were enrolled in a separate Indian Division that worked on reservations. Public Works Administration money nominally outspent the CCC, CWA and WPA combined at Rainier — a figure Catton calls deceiving, since much of it continued the 1920s road program — but it is the Corps’ log cabins, stone comfort stations and stone guardrails that Catton calls its most enduring legacy. [7]

sources.title: Catton, Wonderland (1996), ch. 11, The Impact of the New Deal

women.html: On the afternoon of August 10, 1890, Fay Fuller, a nineteen-year-old Tacoma schoolteacher, stood on the summit in ankle-length bloomers after a two-day climb with four men — the first woman known to have reached the top. Three summers earlier a party had let her come along only on condition that she turn back at 8,500 feet; she went home resolved to go as high as she could. Guide Leonard Longmire, remembering her in 1933, said she rode astride rather than sidesaddle and drilled with rifles alongside a group of young Tacoma women who called themselves the Women’s Guard — behaviour, Potts suggests, that drew criticism from townspeople. Her published account drew fresh attention to the mountain and to mountaineering, particularly for women. [6]

sources.title: Potts, Fay Fuller: First Woman to the Top of Mount Rainier, Columbia: The Magazine of Northwest History (Winter 1996–97), pp. 24–25

MORR.name: Morristown National Historical Park
MORR.summary: Morristown National Historical Park in Morristown, New Jersey, was the first national historical park in the United States, established on March 2, 1933. The park preserves sites associated with two critical winter encampments of the Continental Army during the American Revolution. During the winter of 1779–1780, General George Washington quartered his army of approximately 10,000 soldiers at Jockey Hollow, where they endured what was recorded as the coldest winter of the 18th century — with 28 snowstorms and temperatures colder than at Valley Forge. Washington used the nearby Ford Mansion as his headquarters. The park also preserves Fort Nonsense and the New Jersey Brigade encampment area.

MUWO.name: Muir Woods National Monument
MUWO.summary: Muir Woods National Monument in Marin County, California, protects 554 acres of old-growth coast redwood forest in a sheltered valley on the Pacific coast just north of San Francisco. The monument was established by President Theodore Roosevelt in 1908 after Congressman William Kent and his wife Elizabeth Thacher Kent purchased the land to save it from logging and donated it to the federal government. Kent requested that the monument be named in honor of naturalist John Muir, who called it "the best tree-lovers monument that could possibly be found in all the forests of the world." Some of the redwood trees in the monument are over 250 feet tall and more than 1,000 years old. The monument is part of the Golden Gate National Recreation Area and was designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site component in the Redwood National and State Parks serial nomination.

NAMA.name: National Mall
NAMA.summary: The National Mall and Memorial Parks encompasses some of America's most iconic public spaces and monuments in the heart of Washington, D.C. The Mall stretches approximately two miles from the U.S. Capitol to the Lincoln Memorial and includes the Washington Monument, the World War II Memorial, the Vietnam Veterans Memorial, the Korean War Veterans Memorial, and the Martin Luther King Jr. Memorial, among others. Pierre Charles L'Enfant's 1791 plan for the federal city envisioned the Mall as a grand public promenade, though the space took its current form largely through the McMillan Plan of 1901–1902. The Mall has served as the nation's premier stage for public assembly and free expression, hosting events from Marian Anderson's 1939 concert to the 1963 March on Washington where Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. delivered his "I Have a Dream" speech.

NATR.name: Natchez Trace Parkway
NATR.summary: The Natchez Trace Parkway is a 444-mile scenic road that follows the approximate route of the historic Natchez Trace, an ancient travel corridor connecting Natchez, Mississippi, to Nashville, Tennessee. The original trace was used for thousands of years by Native Americans, including the Natchez, Chickasaw, and Choctaw nations, and became a major route for "Kaintuck" boatmen who floated goods down the Mississippi River to Natchez or New Orleans and then walked home overland. The trace's peak use was between 1785 and 1820, before steamboats made the return trip upriver practical. The parkway, administered by the National Park Service, was authorized in 1938 and substantially completed in 2005, passing through diverse landscapes from cypress swamps to Appalachian foothills.

NRSS.name: Natural Resource Stewardship
NRSS.summary: The National Park Service's natural resource stewardship mission dates to the agency's founding in 1916, when the Organic Act charged the NPS with conserving "the scenery and the natural and historic objects and the wild life therein" for the enjoyment of future generations. The NPS Natural Resource Stewardship and Science Directorate oversees programs in biological resources, geologic resources, water resources, air quality, climate change science, and inventory and monitoring across more than 400 park units. These scientific programs produce peer-reviewed research that informs park management decisions and contributes to the broader scientific understanding of ecosystem health, biodiversity, and environmental change across the nation's most protected landscapes.

ORPI.name: Organ Pipe Cactus National Monument
ORPI.summary: Organ Pipe Cactus National Monument in southwestern Arizona protects 330,689 acres of Sonoran Desert wilderness along the U.S.–Mexico border — the only place in the United States where the organ pipe cactus grows wild. Proclaimed a national monument in 1937, the park was designated a UNESCO International Biosphere Reserve in 1976 in recognition of its outstanding desert ecosystem biodiversity. The monument harbors 28 species of cactus, over 270 species of birds, and rare mammals including the Sonoran pronghorn, one of the most endangered land mammals in North America. The Tohono O'odham people have lived in and around the monument's lands for centuries and maintain cultural connections to the landscape. The monument's location on the international border has made it a focal point in immigration and border security debates.

PETE.name: Petersburg National Battlefield
PETE.summary: Petersburg National Battlefield in Virginia preserves the sites associated with the Siege of Petersburg, a nine-month campaign from June 1864 to April 1865 that ultimately led to the end of the Civil War. General Ulysses S. Grant's strategy to cut the vital railroad supply lines feeding the Confederate capital at Richmond resulted in one of the war's longest sustained operations, with miles of trenches foreshadowing the trench warfare of World War I. The siege included the Battle of the Crater on July 30, 1864, in which Union forces detonated a mine beneath Confederate lines — an assault that ended in a disastrous Union defeat and particularly heavy casualties among United States Colored Troops. The fall of Petersburg on April 2, 1865, led directly to the evacuation of Richmond and Lee's surrender at Appomattox a week later.

REER.name: Reconstruction Era Historical Park (National Monument)
REER.summary: Reconstruction Era National Historical Park in Beaufort County, South Carolina, was established in 2017 as the first unit of the National Park System dedicated to the Reconstruction era (1861–1900). The park preserves sites in and around Beaufort associated with the transition from slavery to freedom, including the Brick Baptist Church — where formerly enslaved people first learned to read — and the Darrah Hall at Penn Center, one of the first schools for freed African Americans in the South. The Sea Islands of South Carolina were among the earliest places where the federal government experimented with programs for formerly enslaved people, including land redistribution, education, and political participation. The park tells the stories of newly freed people who built schools, churches, and communities and exercised their rights as citizens during this transformative period.

RIRA.name: River Raisin National Battlefield Park
RIRA.summary: River Raisin National Battlefield Park in Monroe, Michigan, preserves the site of the January 1813 battles that were among the deadliest engagements of the War of 1812 on American soil. On January 22, 1813, a combined British and Native American force defeated a larger American army along the River Raisin, and the following day, wounded American prisoners were killed in what became known as the River Raisin Massacre — the deadliest single event for U.S. forces in the war. The rallying cry "Remember the Raisin!" became a powerful recruiting tool for the American war effort. The park was designated a national battlefield park in 2010, making it the 392nd unit of the National Park System and the only national battlefield park dedicated to the War of 1812.

ROCR.name: Rock Creek Park
ROCR.summary: Rock Creek Park in Washington, D.C., is one of the largest and oldest urban parks in the United States. Established by an act of Congress in 1890 — just two years after Yellowstone — the park preserves nearly 1,800 acres of forested valley along Rock Creek and its tributaries in the heart of the nation's capital. The park was created to protect the creek's watershed and provide a natural retreat for city residents during the rapid urbanization of late 19th-century Washington. Rock Creek Park includes the Civil War-era Fort DeRussy, Peirce Mill (a 19th-century grist mill), and significant archaeological sites with evidence of Native American habitation dating back thousands of years. The park's forests, trails, and Nature Center make it a vital green space in one of the country's most densely developed metropolitan areas.

SAAN.name: San Antonio Missions National Historical Park
SAAN.summary: San Antonio Missions National Historical Park in San Antonio, Texas, preserves four of the five Spanish colonial missions established along the San Antonio River in the 18th century: Mission Concepción, Mission San José, Mission San Juan, and Mission Espada. Together with the Alamo (Mission San Antonio de Valero), these missions represent the largest concentration of Spanish colonial missions in North America. Founded between 1718 and 1731 by Franciscan friars, the missions served as centers for converting and acculturating Native American peoples into Spanish colonial society. The park was established in 1978 and the missions were inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2015 — the first World Heritage Site in Texas — recognized for their outstanding example of the interchange of Spanish and Coahuiltecan cultures.

SAJH.name: San Juan Island National Historical Park
SAJH.summary: San Juan Island National Historical Park in Washington State preserves the sites of the 1859 Pig War confrontation between the United States and Great Britain over possession of the San Juan Islands. The dispute began when an American settler shot a British-owned pig and escalated into a military standoff with both nations deploying forces on the island. The conflict was resolved through 12 years of joint military occupation and ultimately settled by international arbitration in 1872, when Kaiser Wilhelm I of Germany ruled in favor of the United States. The park preserves both the American Camp and English Camp — the respective military installations — and the island's prairie, forest, and shoreline ecosystems. The park was established in 1966.

SAND.name: Sand Creek Massacre National Historic Site
SAND.summary: Sand Creek Massacre National Historic Site in southeastern Colorado preserves the location where, on November 29, 1864, approximately 675 U.S. volunteer soldiers attacked a peaceful encampment of Cheyenne and Arapaho people, killing an estimated 150 to 200 men, women, children, and elders. The village, led by Chiefs Black Kettle and Left Hand, had been assured of safety by U.S. military officials, and an American flag and a white flag of surrender flew over the camp during the attack. The massacre was condemned by some contemporaries, including a Congressional investigation, but no perpetrators were prosecuted. The site was designated a national historic site in 2007 after extensive consultation with descendants of the Cheyenne and Arapaho victims, who participated in identifying the massacre location.

SARI.name: Salt River Bay National Historical Park and Ecological Preserve
SARI.summary: Salt River Bay National Historical Park and Ecological Preserve on the island of St. Croix in the U.S. Virgin Islands is the only known site where members of a Columbus expedition set foot on what is now U.S. territory. On November 14, 1493, during Columbus's second voyage, a landing party encountered the Kalinago (Carib) people in Salt River Bay — the encounter turned violent and is considered the first documented armed conflict between Europeans and Native Americans. The site also preserves a ceremonial ball court and village site of the Taino people, who inhabited the island before European contact. Established as a national historical park in 1992, Salt River Bay protects one of the largest remaining mangrove forests in the Virgin Islands and a rich marine ecosystem including coral reefs, seagrass beds, and a submarine canyon.

SCBL.name: Scotts Bluff National Monument
SCBL.summary: Scotts Bluff National Monument in western Nebraska preserves a prominent natural landmark along the North Platte River that served as a major waypoint on the Oregon Trail, California Trail, and Mormon Trail during the great westward migrations of the 19th century. The bluff, rising 800 feet above the river valley, was visible for miles and marked the passage through a gap in the series of steep bluffs that forced travelers to find specific routes through the terrain. An estimated 250,000 emigrants passed through Mitchell Pass at the base of the bluff between the 1840s and 1860s, and deep wagon wheel ruts are still visible today. The monument was established in 1919 and includes a museum with one of the finest collections of watercolors by pioneer artist William Henry Jackson.

SEMO.name: Selma to Montgomery NHT
SEMO.summary: The Selma to Montgomery National Historic Trail in Alabama traces the 54-mile route of the 1965 Voting Rights marches from Selma to the state capital in Montgomery — a watershed moment in the American civil rights movement. The first march on March 7, 1965 — "Bloody Sunday" — ended when state and local police attacked approximately 600 peaceful marchers with billy clubs and tear gas at the Edmund Pettus Bridge in Selma, an event broadcast on national television that shocked the nation. Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. led a subsequent march that successfully reached Montgomery on March 25, 1965, with 25,000 supporters. The marches directly led to President Lyndon B. Johnson signing the Voting Rights Act of 1965, one of the most significant pieces of civil rights legislation in American history. The trail was designated in 1996.

SITK.name: Sitka National Historical Park
SITK.summary: Sitka National Historical Park in Sitka, Alaska, is the oldest federally designated park in Alaska, established as a public park in 1890 and redesignated a national monument in 1910 and a national historical park in 1972. The park preserves the site of the 1804 Battle of Sitka — the last major armed resistance by the Tlingit people against Russian colonization in Alaska. The battle occurred when Tlingit warriors defended a wooden fort (the Shís'gi Noow) against a combined Russian and Aleut force; after several days of fighting, the Tlingit withdrew in a strategic retreat. The park also houses the Southeast Alaska Indian Cultural Center, where Tlingit, Haida, and Tsimshian artists practice and demonstrate traditional carving, weaving, and other art forms, and maintains a renowned collection of totem poles along a temperate rainforest trail.

SLBE.name: Sleeping Bear Dunes National Lakeshore
SLBE.summary: Sleeping Bear Dunes National Lakeshore on the northeastern coast of Lake Michigan in Michigan protects 35 miles of shoreline, massive perched sand dunes rising up to 450 feet above the lake, pristine inland lakes, dense beech-maple forests, and two offshore wilderness islands — North and South Manitou. The national lakeshore was established in 1970, and in 2011 viewers of ABC's "Good Morning America" voted its beaches the "Most Beautiful Place in America." The park's name derives from a Chippewa (Ojibwe) legend in which a mother bear and her two cubs swam across Lake Michigan to escape a forest fire; the mother bear waited on the bluff for her cubs, who drowned and became the Manitou Islands, while she became the Sleeping Bear Dune. The park's diverse ecosystems support endangered piping plovers and over 100 species of migratory birds.

STRI.name: Stones River NB
STRI.summary: Stones River National Battlefield near Murfreesboro, Tennessee, preserves the site of the Battle of Stones River (also known as the Battle of Murfreesboro), fought from December 31, 1862, to January 2, 1863. The battle was among the bloodiest of the Civil War, with roughly 23,000 combined casualties — a casualty rate comparable to the Battle of Antietam. The Union victory under Major General William S. Rosecrans secured central Tennessee for the Union and provided a critical morale boost following the Confederate victory at Fredericksburg. The Stones River National Cemetery, established in 1865 at the battlefield, is the oldest national cemetery in the country established during the Civil War. The site was established as a national battlefield in 1927.

TAPR.name: Tallgrass Prairie National Preserve
TAPR.summary: Tallgrass Prairie National Preserve in the Flint Hills of east-central Kansas protects a remnant of the tallgrass prairie ecosystem that once covered 170 million acres of North America — from Indiana to Kansas and from Canada to Texas. Less than 4 percent of the original tallgrass prairie remains today, making it one of the most endangered ecosystems on the continent, and the Flint Hills contain the largest remaining expanse. The preserve was established in 1996 through a public-private partnership between the National Park Service and The Nature Conservancy. The nearly 11,000-acre site includes the historic Spring Hill/Z Bar Ranch with an 1881 limestone ranch house, a massive stone barn, and a one-room schoolhouse. A bison herd was reintroduced to the preserve in 2009.

THRO.name: Theodore Roosevelt National Park
THRO.summary: Theodore Roosevelt National Park in the badlands of western North Dakota memorializes the 26th president and the landscape that profoundly influenced his conservation philosophy. Roosevelt first came to the Dakota Territory in 1883 to hunt bison and subsequently established two cattle ranches — the Maltese Cross and Elkhorn — in the Little Missouri River badlands. His experiences with the harsh beauty of the landscape and his witness to the decimation of wildlife and open range shaped his lifelong commitment to conservation. As president from 1901 to 1909, Roosevelt established the United States Forest Service, created 5 national parks, 18 national monuments, 51 bird reserves, and 150 national forests, protecting roughly 230 million acres. The park was designated a national memorial park in 1947 and redesignated a national park in 1978.

VICK.name: Vicksburg National Military Park
VICK.summary: Vicksburg National Military Park in Vicksburg, Mississippi, preserves the site of the decisive Civil War campaign and 47-day siege that gave the Union control of the Mississippi River. After months of failed approaches, General Ulysses S. Grant executed a brilliant campaign in the spring of 1863, crossing the river south of Vicksburg, winning five battles in 17 days, and laying siege to the city's defenses. The Confederate garrison surrendered on July 4, 1863 — one day after the Union victory at Gettysburg — and President Abraham Lincoln declared that "The Father of Waters again goes unvexed to the sea." The park, established in 1899, contains over 1,340 monuments, markers, and plaques; a restored Union gunboat (the USS Cairo); and the Vicksburg National Cemetery with over 17,000 Union graves.

VIIS.name: Virgin Islands National Park
VIIS.summary: Virgin Islands National Park on the island of St. John in the U.S. Virgin Islands protects approximately 7,259 acres of tropical landscapes and 5,650 acres of submerged marine areas, covering about 60 percent of the island. The park was established in 1956, largely through land donations by Laurance S. Rockefeller, who purchased large tracts of the island to prevent commercial development. The park encompasses white sand beaches, tropical forest, coral reefs, and significant cultural sites including the ruins of colonial-era sugar plantations that were built and operated by enslaved Africans. The 1733 slave revolt on St. John — one of the first and longest slave revolts in the Americas — is an important part of the island's history. Trunk Bay's underwater snorkeling trail is one of the most popular attractions in the U.S. Virgin Islands.

WICA.name: Wind Cave National Park
WICA.summary: Wind Cave National Park in the southern Black Hills of South Dakota protects one of the longest and most complex caves in the world, with over 160 miles of explored passageways, as well as one of the largest remaining mixed-grass prairies in the United States. Wind Cave is distinguished by its extensive boxwork formations — thin calcite fins resembling honeycomb — found in greater quantity here than in any other known cave. The cave is considered sacred by the Lakota people, who know it as "Washun Niya" (the Breathing Hole), and it figures prominently in their creation story as the place from which the Lakota people emerged into the world. Wind Cave was established as the seventh national park in 1903 by President Theodore Roosevelt, making it the first cave to be designated a national park anywhere in the world. The park's surface also supports a free-ranging bison herd descended from animals reintroduced from the Bronx Zoo in 1913.

YOSE.name: Yosemite NP
YOSE.summary: Yosemite National Park in California's Sierra Nevada protects nearly 750,000 acres of granite cliffs, waterfalls, giant sequoia groves, and diverse biological habitat. Yosemite Valley, carved by glaciers over millions of years, features iconic landmarks including El Capitan, Half Dome, and Yosemite Falls — at 2,425 feet, the tallest waterfall in North America. The valley was granted to California as a public trust by President Abraham Lincoln in 1864 — the first time the federal government set aside scenic land specifically for public enjoyment — and was established as a national park in 1890 through the advocacy of John Muir and others. The park is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and is home to the Ahwahneechee people, who have inhabited the valley for at least 3,000 years. Yosemite's scenery has profoundly influenced American art and conservation philosophy, notably through the photography of Ansel Adams.
